terms.define: A sound made with open air and no touch in the mouth, such as a, e or o.
A sound made when the mouth blocks or narrows the air, such as p, s or m.
A consonant where the air stops for a moment and then bursts out, such as p, t or k.
A sound where the air goes out through the nose, such as m or n.
A consonant where the tongue taps many times very fast, like a rolled r.
A consonant where the tongue touches one time, very fast, like a light r.
A consonant where the air is pushed through a narrow gap and makes a hiss, such as f or s.
A consonant that starts as a plosive and ends as a fricative, like ch in chair.
A consonant where the mouth gets close but the air still flows smoothly, such as y or w.
A consonant where the air flows along the sides of the tongue, such as l.
A short sound that works like a vowel but acts like a consonant, such as y or w.
A sound made with both lips, such as p, b or m.
A sound made with the lower lip and the upper teeth, such as f or v.
A sound made with the tongue on the teeth.
A sound made with the tongue on the ridge behind the upper teeth, such as t, d or n.
A sound made with the tongue just behind that ridge, such as sh.
A sound made with the middle of the tongue on the hard roof of the mouth.
A sound made with the back of the tongue on the soft part of the roof of the mouth, such as k or g.
A sound made with the back of the tongue near the small hanging part at the back of the mouth.
A sound made deep in the throat, such as h.
A sound where the voice is on. Touch your throat and you feel it shake, as in z.
A sound where the voice is off. Your throat does not shake, as in s.
A sound followed by a small puff of air, like p in pin.
A vowel where the tongue is high and the mouth is nearly closed, such as i or u.
A vowel where the tongue is low and the mouth is wide, such as a.
A vowel between close and open, such as e or o.
A vowel where the tongue is pushed forward, such as i or e.
A vowel where the tongue is in the middle of the mouth.
A vowel where the tongue is pulled back, such as u or o.
Two vowel sounds in one syllable, where the sound glides from the first to the second.
Three vowel sounds in one syllable.
A short, weak vowel in the middle of the mouth, like the a in about.
A vowel where air goes out through the nose and the mouth at the same time.
A sound that you hold for more time.
A sound that you say very quickly.
Two vowels side by side that belong to two different syllables.
One beat of a word. Each syllable has one vowel sound at its centre.
The strength you give to one syllable so that it sounds louder, longer or higher.
A syllable that you say with more strength.
A syllable that you say with less strength.
The way your voice goes up and down over a whole sentence.
How high or low your voice sounds.
A pitch pattern on a syllable that can change the meaning of a word.
The pattern of strong and weak beats in speech.
The smallest sound that can change the meaning of a word.
A written sign of the alphabet.
Two letters that together write one sound, such as sh.
A small mark on a letter, such as an accent.
A diacritic written above a letter, such as in cafe with an accent on the e.
A letter that you write but do not say.
A way to write how a word sounds, using special signs.
The International Phonetic Alphabet. It gives one sign to each sound, for every language.
Two words that differ by only one sound, such as bat and pat.
Two or more consonants side by side with no vowel between them.
A consonant that you hold longer, or say twice.
A consonant said with the middle of the tongue raised toward the roof of the mouth.
A change where one sound becomes more like the sound next to it.
A sound that you leave out in fast speech.
A rule where the vowels in a word must belong to the same group.
A change from one sound to another inside a word.
A final consonant that you say only when the next word starts with a vowel.
The syllable in a word that you say with most strength.
The words in a sentence that you say with most strength.
